canonical_definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats commonsense reasoning as a latent ability to use everyday or general world knowledge, intuition, and shared assumptions about ordinary physical or social situations to make plausible inferences, judgments, or predictions, especially when relevant information is not explicit. Many definitions phrase this as making presumptions about the ordinary world, applying broad knowledge to infer likely outcomes, or filling knowledge gaps through informal reasoning. A smaller line of work defines it more narrowly as the observable task of answering benchmark questions, choosing plausible continuations, or doing sentence completion, and a few papers situate it in specific settings such as embodied task structure, video interpretation, spatial filtering, or cause and effect questions in text. The main disagreement is therefore between a broad latent ability and narrower task- or setting-specific formulations.

Space of facets. Papers use several nearby labels around the same family of phenomena: commonsense inference typically emphasizes plausible unstated conclusions or relations between concepts and events, commonsense understanding emphasizes answering or following instructions that depend on commonsense knowledge, and commonsense grounding emphasizes interpreting and acting in realistic scenarios. One paper explicitly subdivides commonsense reasoning into explanatory, predictive, and counterfactual sub-skills, while another conceptualization ties it to a default world model of background conditions and assumptions. Across these uses, papers often place it near broader reasoning and world-knowledge abilities, but the labels are not used uniformly.

Space of measurement. Operationally, papers link commonsense reasoning to 57 measurement instruments and 9 behavioral indicators. The most recurrent instruments are benchmark datasets, especially HellaSwag, WinoGrande, PIQA, OpenBookQA, and ARC-Challenge; many studies also frame the target behavior as multiple-choice or True/False question answering, sentence completion, or selecting the most plausible continuation, often in zero-shot or few-shot evaluation and sometimes through shared evaluation harnesses or composite benchmark suites. Smaller strands extend measurement to multilingual, multimodal, video, agent, and embodied benchmarks. These operationalizations generally match the task-oriented definitions, but they also narrow broader latent-ability definitions to short-form answer selection or QA accuracy.

Links. Beyond measurement, papers most often report commonsense reasoning as related to reasoning more broadly, and some also relate it to world knowledge and other neighboring reasoning notions. Several single-paper claims also record causal relationships from commonsense reasoning to generalization and other downstream capabilities or behaviors, while separate papers claim causal relationships from in-context learning to commonsense reasoning and from refusal to commonsense reasoning. A smaller line of work uses commonsense reasoning itself as a measure of broader abilities.

characterization_sections.label: Space of definitions.
characterization_sections.text: Across papers, the prevailing usage treats commonsense reasoning as a latent ability to use everyday or general world knowledge, intuition, and shared assumptions about ordinary physical or social situations to make plausible inferences, judgments, or predictions, especially when relevant information is not explicit. Many definitions phrase this as making presumptions about the ordinary world, applying broad knowledge to infer likely outcomes, or filling knowledge gaps through informal reasoning. A smaller line of work defines it more narrowly as the observable task of answering benchmark questions, choosing plausible continuations, or doing sentence completion, and a few papers situate it in specific settings such as embodied task structure, video interpretation, spatial filtering, or cause and effect questions in text. The main disagreement is therefore between a broad latent ability and narrower task- or setting-specific formulations.

characterization_sections.label: Space of facets.
characterization_sections.text: Papers use several nearby labels around the same family of phenomena: commonsense inference typically emphasizes plausible unstated conclusions or relations between concepts and events, commonsense understanding emphasizes answering or following instructions that depend on commonsense knowledge, and commonsense grounding emphasizes interpreting and acting in realistic scenarios. One paper explicitly subdivides commonsense reasoning into explanatory, predictive, and counterfactual sub-skills, while another conceptualization ties it to a default world model of background conditions and assumptions. Across these uses, papers often place it near broader reasoning and world-knowledge abilities, but the labels are not used uniformly.

characterization_sections.label: Space of measurement.
characterization_sections.text: Operationally, papers link commonsense reasoning to 57 measurement instruments and 9 behavioral indicators. The most recurrent instruments are benchmark datasets, especially HellaSwag, WinoGrande, PIQA, OpenBookQA, and ARC-Challenge; many studies also frame the target behavior as multiple-choice or True/False question answering, sentence completion, or selecting the most plausible continuation, often in zero-shot or few-shot evaluation and sometimes through shared evaluation harnesses or composite benchmark suites. Smaller strands extend measurement to multilingual, multimodal, video, agent, and embodied benchmarks. These operationalizations generally match the task-oriented definitions, but they also narrow broader latent-ability definitions to short-form answer selection or QA accuracy.

characterization_sections.label: Links.
characterization_sections.text: Beyond measurement, papers most often report commonsense reasoning as related to reasoning more broadly, and some also relate it to world knowledge and other neighboring reasoning notions. Several single-paper claims also record causal relationships from commonsense reasoning to generalization and other downstream capabilities or behaviors, while separate papers claim causal relationships from in-context learning to commonsense reasoning and from refusal to commonsense reasoning. A smaller line of work uses commonsense reasoning itself as a measure of broader abilities.

definition_agreement.reason: Most papers define commonsense reasoning as the ability to use everyday or real-world knowledge and human-like intuitive assumptions to make plausible inferences, judgments, or predictions about ordinary physical or social situations, often measured through question answering, continuation, or selection tasks. A few papers narrow this to particular settings such as causal text questions, video, spatial, safety, or embodied tasks, but they still treat the same core capability rather than a different phenomenon.

characterization:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats commonsense reasoning as a latent ability to use everyday or general world knowledge, intuition, and shared assumptions about ordinary physical or social situations to make plausible inferences, judgments, or predictions, especially when relevant information is not explicit. Many definitions phrase this as making presumptions about the ordinary world, applying broad knowledge to infer likely outcomes, or filling knowledge gaps through informal reasoning. A smaller line of work defines it more narrowly as the observable task of answering benchmark questions, choosing plausible continuations, or doing sentence completion, and a few papers situate it in specific settings such as embodied task structure, video interpretation, spatial filtering, or cause and effect questions in text. The main disagreement is therefore between a broad latent ability and narrower task- or setting-specific formulations.

Space of facets. Papers use several nearby labels around the same family of phenomena: commonsense inference typically emphasizes plausible unstated conclusions or relations between concepts and events, commonsense understanding emphasizes answering or following instructions that depend on commonsense knowledge, and commonsense grounding emphasizes interpreting and acting in realistic scenarios. One paper explicitly subdivides commonsense reasoning into explanatory, predictive, and counterfactual sub-skills, while another conceptualization ties it to a default world model of background conditions and assumptions. Across these uses, papers often place it near broader reasoning and world-knowledge abilities, but the labels are not used uniformly.

Space of measurement. Operationally, papers link commonsense reasoning to 57 measurement instruments and 9 behavioral indicators. The most recurrent instruments are benchmark datasets, especially HellaSwag, WinoGrande, PIQA, OpenBookQA, and ARC-Challenge; many studies also frame the target behavior as multiple-choice or True/False question answering, sentence completion, or selecting the most plausible continuation, often in zero-shot or few-shot evaluation and sometimes through shared evaluation harnesses or composite benchmark suites. Smaller strands extend measurement to multilingual, multimodal, video, agent, and embodied benchmarks. These operationalizations generally match the task-oriented definitions, but they also narrow broader latent-ability definitions to short-form answer selection or QA accuracy.

Links. Beyond measurement, papers most often report commonsense reasoning as related to reasoning more broadly, and some also relate it to world knowledge and other neighboring reasoning notions. Several single-paper claims also record causal relationships from commonsense reasoning to generalization and other downstream capabilities or behaviors, while separate papers claim causal relationships from in-context learning to commonsense reasoning and from refusal to commonsense reasoning. A smaller line of work uses commonsense reasoning itself as a measure of broader abilities.
